rgb: Across all five frames, the camera wearer looks steeply downward from an egocentric viewpoint at their own torso (3 to 5 metres below the camera) and a green work surface positioned directly in front of and below them at roughly 3 to 5 metres distance, where all tools and parts lie out of arm's reach. Directly beneath and beside the green surface at 3 to 5 metres distance are suspension springs, a blue tarp on the right, and a rusted metal assembly on a cart to the left, while a red car wheel sits 0.5 to 1.5 metres away within reach in the upper-left foreground. depth: The depth map shows a top-down egocentric view where the camera wearer's chest at the bottom is farthest (3–5 m), both arms extend downward and forward (3–5 m) toward a flat green cart tray at roughly 3–5 m, and the garage floor and surrounding vehicle wheels lie nearer and within reach at 0.5–1.5 m. On the tray out of arm's reach, an upright white bottle on the right (frames 2–4) and a cardboard box on a lower cart to the left (frame 5, ~3–5 m away) protrude clearly toward the camera relative to the flat tray surface, while the hands recede farther from the lens in frame 2 (~3–5 m) as they unscrew the bottle cap before moving back down to the tray in frames 3–5. In frame 5, the camera wearer turns and steps slightly left, shifting the green tray to the bottom-right and revealing a lower cart with metal parts, a spare wheel on the floor to the lower-left (~3–5 m), and a second person's legs standing ~0.5–1.5 m away within reach in the upper-left corner facing toward/sideways. Compared to the cluttered RGB image, the depth map makes the vertical elevation step between the upper green tray, the adjacent lower cart, and the floor immediately obvious, as well as the upright height of the white bottle. However, the map is unreliable for thin and flat items on the tray—such as the wire brush, red screwdriver, brake pads, and thin applicator brush held in frames 3–4—which blend into the tray's depth or show blurry, bridged boundaries between the hands and the background.
segmentation: The segmentation map isolates the camera wearer's torso and outstretched arms in the lower background (3–5 m away, out of reach of the tray) across all five frames, and detects the lower legs of a second person standing ~0.5–1.5 m away within reach in the upper-left corner of frame 5. Across frames 1 to 4, the masks track the wearer's right and left arms reaching forward to the upper-right in frame 2, approaching from the right and upper-left in frame 3, and moving apart far from the center in frame 4 before shifting toward the bottom-left in frame 5 as the wearer turns left. It correctly segments the small white lubricant bottle on the right of the tray (~3–5 m away, out of arm's reach) as a 'bottle' in frame 4, helping separate its round top from the cluttered background. However, the segmentation map is highly unreliable across the sequence: it fragments the wearer's single torso and two arms into multiple separate 'person' instances with hard vertical splits, and completely misses the tools, brake pads, and carts. Furthermore, it hallucinates false classes on background objects, mislabeling the blue tarp on the right as a 'person' (frames 2–3), the aerosol can on the upper-left of the tray as a 'cell phone' (frame 2), a car wheel in the upper-left foreground as a 'bicycle' (frame 3), and the green utility tray itself as a 'cake' (frame 5).
pose: The pose map tracks the 3D-projected finger and palm skeletons (magenta) of the camera wearer's right and left hands at roughly 3–5 m in front of and below the head, operating 3–5 m apart above the tray and out of reach. Across the five frames, the hand skeletons show the hands far apart over the center of the tray in frame 1, shifting up and right in frame 2 as the left hand arches over the right to open the bottle, approaching in frame 3 (~3–5 m apart) as the left hand lifts the cap brush to the upper-left while the right rests near the center, moving apart again in frame 4 while coating the metal bracket, and moving down in frame 5. The skeleton wireframes clearly reveal precise finger curl, thumb opposition, and palm orientation even when the hands are partially self-occluded or visually blended against similarly toned rusty metal parts and shadows in the RGB frames. However, the pose map is unreliable in frame 5, where it completely misses the camera wearer's right hand at the bottom-right edge of the frame because the hand is partially cropped by the image boundary. It also fails to detect any yellow body skeleton for the camera wearer's torso and arms (whose shoulders and head are out of view behind the camera) or for the second person whose legs are partially visible in the upper-left corner of frame 5.
